entry: Subgenre of [[Science fiction|science fiction]] set in a dystopian future and characterized by a focus on "lowlife and high tech." Its settings pair advanced technology, including [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] and cyberware, with societal collapse and decay. The genre drew on the 1960s–70s New Wave movement, and William Gibson's *Neuromancer* (1984) helped establish it. The Japanese strand began in 1982 with Katsuhiro Otomo's manga *Akira*, whose 1988 anime film popularized it. Early films include Ridley Scott's *Blade Runner* (1982).

Being with both organic and biomechatronic body parts. The term, a portmanteau of *cybernetic* and *organism*, was coined in 1960 by Manfred Clynes and Nathan S. Kline. Unlike [[Android (robot)|androids]] or biorobots, a cyborg is a living organism whose function has been restored, or whose abilities have been enhanced, by an artificial component that relies on feedback, such as a prosthesis, implant or artificial organ. Cyborgs are commonly thought of as [[Mammal|mammals]], including [[Human|humans]], but the term can apply to any organism.

Division of naked-seeded, dioecious plants that superficially resemble palms. Cycads are seed plants with a stout, woody, usually unbranched [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] crowned by large, hard, evergreen, usually pinnate (feather-shaped) leaves. Individual plants are either male or female, and both sexes bear strobili, somewhat like conifer cones, that hold pollen or seeds. Cycads are [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]] and are not closely related to palms or [[Fern|ferns]], although their similarities arise from convergent evolution. Cycads have specialized pollinators, usually a specific [[Beetle|beetle]], and more rarely a thrips or a moth. Their roots host [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]] that fix nitrogen. Cycads appeared around 300 million years ago and reached their greatest diversity in the [[Mesozoic]]. Four species are on the brink of extinction, and seven have fewer than 100 plants left in the wild. In [[Vanuatu]] the plant symbolizes peace and appears on the national flag.

Competitive physical activity using bicycles. Racing categories include [[Road bicycle racing|road racing]], cyclo-cross, mountain bike racing, track cycling, BMX and cycle speedway, while non-racing sports include artistic cycling, cycle polo, freestyle BMX, mountain bike trials and cycleball. The Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), founded on 14 April 1900, is the world governing body for international competitive [[Cycling|cycling]]. The International Human Powered Vehicle Association governs human-powered vehicles with fewer design restrictions than the UCI, and the UltraMarathon Cycling Association governs many ultra-distance races. Bicycle racing is an Olympic sport and has featured at every [[Summer Olympic Games]] since 1896. Bicycle races are popular worldwide, especially in Europe, where the countries most devoted to the sport include Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland. The first bicycle race is popularly held to have taken place at the Parc de Saint-Cloud, Paris, in 1868.

Activity of riding a [[Bicycle|bicycle]] or other pedal-driven, human-powered vehicle, practised for transport, recreation, exercise and competitive sport. Cycling became popular in Europe and North America in the late 19th century, and over 50% of the human population knows how to ride a bike. Bicycles have been used for reconnaissance and to transport soldiers and supplies. In the [[Second Boer War]] both sides used them for scouting, and in [[World War I]] France, Germany, Australia and New Zealand used them to move troops. In its 1937 invasion of China, Japan employed some 50,000 bicycle troops. Communist forces used bicycles as cargo carriers on the Ho Chi Minh Trail during the [[Vietnam War]]. Switzerland, the last country known to maintain a regiment of bicycle troops, disbanded its last unit in 2003. In many countries the most common road vehicle is the utility bicycle, and Denmark and the Netherlands have the most bicycles per capita in Europe.

Large-scale air mass rotating around a center of low [[Atmospheric pressure|atmospheric pressure]]. Cyclones rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, with winds spiraling inward. The name comes from the Greek *kýklos*, meaning "circle," and was coined by Henry Piddington, who published 40 papers on tropical storms from Calcutta between 1836 and 1855. Cyclones have also been observed on [[Mars]], [[Jupiter]] and Neptune. [[Extratropical cyclone|Extratropical cyclones]] form along baroclinic zones and last two to six days, steered by the subtropical [[Jet stream|jet stream]]. Cold fronts typically feature narrow bands of thunderstorms, while warm fronts are usually preceded by stratiform precipitation and fog. [[Tropical cyclone|Tropical cyclones]] are warm-core systems fueled by latent heat from thunderstorm activity. They are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific, [[Typhoon|typhoons]] in the northwestern Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian and South Pacific oceans. Mesocyclones over land can lead to [[Tornado|tornado]] formation.

High-mass [[X-ray|X-ray]] binary in the constellation [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]], containing a stellar [[Black hole|black hole]]. Discovered in 1964 during a rocket flight, it is one of the strongest X-ray sources detectable from Earth and was the first such source widely accepted to be a black hole. The system pairs a blue supergiant variable star with the black hole, about 0.2 [[Astronomical unit|AU]] apart. A stellar wind from the supergiant feeds an accretion disk around the black hole, where matter heated to millions of degrees emits the observed X-rays. A pair of relativistic jets, arranged perpendicular to the disk, carries part of the infalling material's energy into interstellar space. In 1975 physicist [[Stephen Hawking|Stephen Hawking]] wagered that Cygnus X-1 was not a black hole, hoping to lose. He conceded the bet in 1990, after observational data had strengthened the case for a black hole.

Northern constellation on the plane of the [[Milky Way]], named for the Latinized Greek word for swan. It was among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer [[Ptolemy]] and remains one of the 88 modern constellations. It contains the Northern Cross asterism and Deneb, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. The constellation is also home to [[Cygnus X-1]], the first object widely held to be a [[Black hole|black hole]].

Common [[Percussion instrument|percussion instrument]] made of thin, usually round plates of copper alloy, often played in pairs. Most cymbals have indefinite pitch and are used in [[Orchestra|orchestras]], percussion ensembles, jazz, rock and marching bands. Drum kits usually include a crash, ride or crash/ride cymbal and a pair of hi-hat cymbals. The name derives from the Latin *cymbalum*, from the Greek *kymbalon*, related to *kymbē*, "cup" or "bowl." Cymbals appear in reliefs from the Armenian Highlands (7th century BC), [[Assyria]], ancient Egypt, [[Ancient Greece|Greece]] and Rome, and are mentioned in the [[Bible]]. Turkish janissaries used cymbals in the 14th century or earlier, and by the 17th century they were part of European music. The bell, the raised area around the central hole, produces a higher pitch than the rest of the plate.

American singer, songwriter and actress known for eccentric clothing and a four-octave vocal range. Her debut album, *She's So Unusual* (1983), earned Best New Artist at the 1985 [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], and the video for its single "Girls Just Want to Have Fun" won Best Female Video at the inaugural 1984 [[MTV|MTV]] Video Music Awards. Lauper composed the score for the Broadway musical *Kinky Boots*, winning a Tony Award in 2013 as the first woman to win the category alone. She has sold over 50 million records and received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame|Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Family of grass-like [[Monocotyledon|monocotyledonous]] flowering plants known as sedges. It contains around 5,500 described species in about 90 genera; the largest, with over 2,000 species, is *Carex*, the "true sedges." Sedges are widely distributed, with their greatest diversity in [[East Asia]], and most species prefer temperate climates. Many thrive in [[Wetland|wetlands]] or poor soils. Their stems have triangular cross-sections and their leaves are arranged in three ranks, giving the mnemonic "sedges have edges." The papyrus sedge, *Cyperus papyrus*, is the plant from which [[Papyrus|papyrus]] was made. Members form dauciform, carrot-shaped roots, analogous to the cluster roots of [[Proteaceae]], that help them take up [[Phosphorus]] from poor soil. Sedges appear in the fossil record from the [[Eocene]] epoch, with earlier fossils from the Late [[Cretaceous]].

Order of [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fishes]] including barbs, loaches, carps and minnows. It contains 11–12 families (some authorities list up to 23), more than 400 genera and over 4,250 named species, and lies within the superorder Ostariophysi. Most are freshwater fishes. The family Cyprinidae, the [[Carp|carps]] and minnows, makes up about two-thirds of the order's diversity; cyprinids are most diverse in [[Southeast Asia]] and are absent from Australia and South America. The mouth has no teeth; instead, pharyngeal teeth in the throat grind against a chewing pad on the skull. Their closest living relatives are the [[Characiformes]], the Gymnotiformes (electric eel and American knifefishes) and the Siluriformes (catfishes). At 112 years, the bigmouth buffalo is the longest-lived cypriniform fish documented.

Order of [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fishes]], mostly small and freshwater, including many popular aquarium fish such as killifish and live-bearers. Informally called toothcarps, they are not close relatives of the true [[Carp|carps]], which belong to the superorder Ostariophysi. Species are informally grouped by reproductive strategy: some are egg-laying (oviparous), while others bear live young, either ovoviviparously or viviparously. Typically [[Carnivore|carnivores]], they often live near the surface and eat insects, worms and aquatic crustaceans. Killifish obtain some [[Carotenoid|carotenoids]] for their body pigments from pollen on the insects they eat. The largest species, the cuatro ojos (*Anableps dowei*), measures 34 cm (13 in), while the least killifish (*Heterandria formosa*) is 8 mm (0.31 in) as an adult. The oldest fossils are scales from the Late Paleocene of Argentina.

Island country in the eastern [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], off the coast of the [[Levant]]. The capital is [[Nicosia]]. The island is divided along a [[United Nations]] buffer zone between the Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which only [[Turkey]] recognizes. Settled about 13,000 years ago, Cyprus was seized from Persian control by [[Alexander the Great]] in 333 BC, and it was under Ottoman rule from 1571 to 1878. It was annexed by the United Kingdom in 1914 and became independent in 1960. Greek Cypriots sought union with Greece (*enosis*), while Turkish Cypriots pursued partition (*taksim*). After a coup on 15 July 1974 by Greek Cypriot nationalists and elements of the Greek military junta, a Turkish invasion displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots. The division remains subject to an ongoing dispute. Cyprus joined the [[European Union]] in 2004 and the [[Euro|eurozone]] in 2008.

Fifth president of [[South Africa]] since 2018 and president of the [[African National Congress]] (ANC). A former anti-apartheid activist and [[Trade union|trade union]] leader, he was elected ANC secretary general in 1991 under [[Nelson Mandela]] and was the party's chief negotiator in talks that ended apartheid. After leaving politics in 1996 for business, he was deputy president from 2014 to 2018 and was elected ANC president in 2017. He chaired the [[African Union]] from 2020 to 2021 and led South Africa's response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].

Brothers and Byzantine Christian theologians and missionaries of the 9th century. Known as the "Apostles to the [[Slavs|Slavs]]," they are credited with devising the Glagolitic alphabet, the first alphabet used to transcribe Old Church Slavonic. Around 860, Emperor Michael III and Patriarch Photius sent Cyril on a mission to the [[Khazars]]. In 862 the brothers began work in [[Great Moravia]] at the request of Prince Rastislav, whose motives were probably more political than religious. Their pupils continued the missionary work among other Slavs after the brothers' deaths. Both are venerated as saints in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]]. In 1980 [[Pope John Paul II]], the first Slav pope, declared them co-patron saints of Europe with [[Benedict of Nursia]].

Egyptian Christian theologian and Patriarch of [[Alexandria]] from 412 to 444. He was a central figure in the Christological controversies of the late 4th and 5th centuries. As president of the Council of Ephesus in 431, he helped clarify the hypostatic union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person, against the views of Nestorius, who was deposed as Patriarch of [[Constantinople]]. He advocated the term *Theotokos* for the Virgin Mary. Cyril is venerated as a saint in the [[Catholic Church|Catholic]] and Orthodox churches, and Pope Leo XIII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1883. His tenure included a long dispute with the imperial prefect Orestes over ecclesiastical and civil authority in the city.

[[Writing system|Writing system]] used for many languages across [[Eurasia|Eurasia]], including Slavic, Turkic and Mongolic languages. As of 2019, around 250 million people used it as the official script for their national languages, with Russia accounting for about half. When Bulgaria joined the [[European Union]] in 2007, Cyrillic became the third official script of the EU, after the Latin and Greek alphabets. The Early Cyrillic alphabet was developed in the 9th century at the Preslav Literary School in the [[First Bulgarian Empire]], probably by disciples of [[Cyril and Methodius]], and is named in honor of Saint Cyril. Derived from the Greek uncial script, it was augmented with letters from the Glagolitic alphabet for sounds absent in Greek. It spread among other [[Slavs|Slavs]] and non-Slavic Romanians, and came to dominate Glagolitic in the 12th century.

Inherited genetic disorder, mainly affecting the [[Lung|lungs]] and [[Pancreas|pancreas]]. Caused by [[Mutation|mutations]] in both copies of the [[Gene|gene]] for the CFTR protein, it makes thick mucus accumulate in the lungs, leaving them prone to infection by bacteria such as [[Staphylococcus aureus|Staphylococcus aureus]] and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Diagnosis relies on a sweat test that measures [[Chloride|chloride]] levels. There is no known cure, but CFTR modulators and [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] have substantially improved survival, and lung problems account for approximately 30% of deaths. Median survival is approximately 65 years in Canada, the U.S. and the U.K.

Material within a [[Cell (biology)|cell]], enclosed by the [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]] and excluding the nucleus in eukaryotes. Its main components are the cytosol, a gel-like substance, the cell's internal structures and various inclusions. About 80% water and usually colorless, the cytosol suspends larger structures such as [[Ribosome|ribosomes]], [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]], plastids, lipid droplets and vacuoles. Many cellular activities take place in the cytoplasm, including [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]], [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and cell division. The movement of [[Calcium|calcium]] ions into and out of the cytoplasm is a signaling activity for metabolic processes. Cytoplasmic streaming, the movement of the cytoplasm around organelles, occurs in large animal and plant cells, amoebae and slime molds. The term was introduced by Rudolf von Kölliker in 1863.

Dynamic network of [[Protein|protein]] filaments in the [[Cytoplasm|cytoplasm]] of all [[Cell (biology)|cells]], including those of bacteria and archaea. In [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], it extends from the [[Cell nucleus|nucleus]] to the [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]] and has three main components: microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules. Its primary function is to give the cell its shape and mechanical resistance, and it can contract, allowing cells to migrate. It takes part in cell signaling, endocytosis, the segregation of chromosomes during [[Mitosis|mitosis]], and the intracellular transport of vesicles and organelles. Microfilaments are made of actin, the most abundant cellular protein, and during [[Muscle contraction|muscle contraction]] myosin motors exert force on parallel actin filaments. Tropomyosin inhibits this interaction until troponin, responding to rising calcium, releases the inhibition. Nikolai K. Koltsov proposed the cytoskeleton in 1903, and it was found in prokaryotes in 1992.

Landlocked country in [[Central Europe|Central Europe]], also known as Czechia and historically as Bohemia. Its capital and largest city is [[Prague]]. The Duchy of Bohemia was founded in the 9th century under [[Great Moravia]], and the Czech lands were integrated into the [[Habsburg monarchy]] after 1526. Most of the region became part of the First Czechoslovak Republic in 1918, the only parliamentary democracy in Central and Eastern Europe through the interwar period. After the 1938 Munich Agreement, Nazi Germany took control of the Czech lands. A communist coup in 1948 was followed by the suppression of the [[Prague Spring|Prague Spring]] by a Soviet-led invasion in 1968, and the Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in 1989. Czechoslovakia was dissolved peacefully on 31 December 1992. The Czech Republic is a unitary parliamentary republic and developed high-income economy, and a member of [[NATO|NATO]] and the [[European Union|European Union]].

[[Slavic languages|West Slavic]] language of the Czech–Slovak group, written in the [[Latin alphabet|Latin script]]. It is the official language of the [[Czech Republic|Czech Republic]] and is spoken by over 12 million people, including second-language speakers. Czech is closely related to Slovak and, to a lesser degree, to Polish. It is a fusional language with a rich system of [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]] and relatively flexible word order, and its vocabulary has been extensively influenced by Latin and German. The modern written standard was codified during the Czech National Revival in the late 18th to mid-19th century. The most widely spoken non-standard variety, Common Czech, is based on the vernacular of [[Prague|Prague]]. Czech has ten monophthongs, three diphthongs and 25 consonants, and a raised alveolar trill, written ř, that occurs as a phoneme in few other languages. [[Jan Hus|Jan Hus]] contributed significantly to the standardization of Czech orthography.

Former country in [[Central Europe|Central Europe]], 1918–1992. It declared independence in 1918 amid the dissolution of [[Austria-Hungary|Austria-Hungary]], and its sovereignty was affirmed by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye. Championed by its first presidents, Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš, it was the only functioning parliamentary democracy in Central and Eastern Europe during the interwar period. After the 1938 Munich Agreement, the Sudetenland was annexed by [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]], and the state ceased to exist under German occupation. Re-established after liberation by the Red Army, it became part of the [[Eastern Bloc|Eastern Bloc]] after a communist coup in 1948 and joined the [[Warsaw Pact|Warsaw Pact]] in 1955. The [[Prague Spring|Prague Spring]] reforms were ended by a Soviet-led invasion in 1968, and the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule. The country split peacefully into the [[Czech Republic|Czech Republic]] and Slovakia on 31 December 1992.

American comic book publisher, one of the largest and oldest in the country. Its name is an initialism for *Detective Comics*, first published in 1937. Most of its stories are set in the fictional DC Universe, which features [[Superman|Superman]], [[Batman|Batman]] and [[Wonder Woman|Wonder Woman]]. Together with its rival [[Marvel Comics|Marvel]], DC held approximately 70% of the American comic book market in 2017, a figure that excludes graphic novel sales. The company has also published *Watchmen* and *V for Vendetta* under its Vertigo and DC Black Label imprints. As of 2025, DC was the second-largest comic book publisher in the comic book shop market, after Marvel.
